This was one half ofthe Archbishop of Canterbury’s Hundred of Loxfield (Lochesfeld 1130 P, Lockesfeld, Lokkesfeld 1248 Ass, 1272 RH), the DB Hundred of Malling (Mellinges). In the 16th cent. that hundred was divided into two parts. One be- came Loxfield Dorset infra 389, the other appears as Loxfield- Neville, Loxfield-Baker (1624 SAC 21, 12), -Pelham (1630 SAC 16, 49) and, when acquired by the Marquis of Camden, as -Camden (1790 SAC 21, 9)®. XLIT. LOXFIELD DORSET HUNDRED For the origin of this hundred, v. Loxfield Camden supra 380.

For the origin of this hundred, v. Loxfield Camden supra 380. In the 16th century some of the Archbishop’s manors were exchanged with the Queen for other manors, and some were granted to the Sackvilles (afterwards earls of Dorset).

When the hundred was divided this part became known as Loxfield Dorset. In the Subsidy Rolls for Framfield (1296, 1327, 1332) we have John and Matilda de Lockesfeld and Robert de Lockes- feld and in 1440 we have Lokkysfeld (Ct) and in 1639 and 1642 Loxefielde, Lockfield in Framfield (SRS 14, 124), so that the meeting-place for the whole Hundred was probably at the Hundred House in that parish.

FLIMWELL is Flimenwelle 1210 KAC 6, 218, Flemenewett 1288 Ass, c. 1330 LibP (all p), Flemyngwell 1309 Cl, Flimwell 1409 BM. ‘Fugitives’ spring,’ from OE fliemena-wielle (v. wielle). The significance of the name lies in the fact that the place is just within the county border and here doubtless fugitives from one county to the other could first get refreshment. Cf: to wreccena wyllan (BCS 764) with a similar meaning, wrecca de-noting ‘an exile,’ ‘a miserable person.’

Row ey is the runanleagesmearc of 1018 (O.S. Facs iii. 39). The latter is clearly to be identified with the home of Elia de Runle (1296 SR), John de Rumlegh and Elia de Rondlegh (1327 SR), and John de Rondlegh (1332 SR). The first element is a pers. name Rina, a pet-form of an OE name beginning with Ran-. The later development is difficult. The vowel must have re- mained long, Rianan becoming Rie (roune), while later nl became d/. Rowdley was then assimilated to the very common Rowley type.

SENLAC or SANDLAKE (lost) Santlache 12th Bello Senlac 12th Ord Sandlak(e), (borga de) 1248 AOMB 18, 1296, 1332 SR, 1398 BM et passim to 1667 Battle Seynlak 1343 Battle 72 Sanglake 1516 AOMB 56 ‘Sand-stream’ or ‘sand-water-course,’ v. sand, lacu. The main street which skirts the abbey precincts is still called ‘Upper and Lower Lake.’ This is given as the name of the famous battle by Orderic, using a spelling which shows common AN confusion of a and e. This form was first adopted from Orderic as the name of the battle by the historian Freeman and has continued in use in our histories (v. the full discussion by Stevenson in EHR 28, 292). In earlier days attempts were made to explain the name in a way which would fit the events in more picturesque fashion. Thus Camden (317) writes ‘Wherein (i.e. in Battle) there is a place called by a French word sangue lac, of the bloud there shed, which by nature of the ground seemeth after raine to wax red.” The form Sanglake is found in 1724 on a map of the manor of Battle. As a matter of fact the little stream here is of chalybeate origin and does run red after heavy rain (v. EHR 28, 301).
